Design: Fifteen common objects secured on a palpation board
were covered with a blinding thin fabric. The boards were then
palpated by 89 osteopathic students, fellows, and physicians at an
osteopathic conference. The participants were then asked to ﬁll out
a questionnaire regarding the 15 objects palpated. Information
regarding the current level of experience was also recorded.
Setting: Osteopathic educational conference.
Participants: 89 osteopathic medical students, fellows, and phy-
sicians.
Interventions: Assessment of palpation skill of blinded objects.
Main Outcome Measures: Determine if experience in osteo-
pathic manipulation improves accuracy in palpation of objects.
Results: No difference was found among the palpatory skills tested
between osteopathic medical students, fellows, and physicians.
However, palpatory skills between osteopathic medical students
and osteopathic teaching fellows approached signiﬁcance
(P/H11005.055). In addition, palpatory skills between medical students in
their ﬁrst 2 years and medical students in their last 2 years also
approached signiﬁcance (P/H11005.057).
Conclusions: Palpatory skills of inanimate objects do not differ
among osteopathic practitioners with various levels of experience.
However, patient palpation skills and the relationship to osteo-
pathic experience cannot be concluded. Palpation of patients may
require a subset of palpatory skills not tested in this study, because
osteopathic manipulative treatments provide healing, which occurs
beyond the interface of the hand-to-patient contact.
Poster 408
Severe Spasticity in a Patient With Stiff Person
Syndrome: A Case Report.
Reekesh Patel, MD (Tufts Medical Center, Boston, MA,
United States); Maturin Finch, MD, Akbar Khan, DO,
Kareen A. Velez, MD.
Disclosures: R. Patel, none.
Patients or Programs: A 59-year-old woman with a 10-year
history of stiff person syndrome (SPS).
Program Description: The patient presented to an inpatient
rehabilitation facility with pain, tremors, spasticity, stiffness, and
jerking and/or myoclonic movements that hindered ambulation.
She had greater left lower extremity spasticity when compared with
the right. Hence, she was started on a comprehensive, multidisci-
plinary movement disorder rehabilitation program.
Setting: Inpatient rehabilitation facility.
Results: Patient’s dystonic and myoclonic symptoms improved
with levetiracetam. She was treated with diazepam and baclofen for
spasticity management, without signiﬁcant results. The patient was
unable to tolerate physical activity secondary to worsening pain and
spasticity. Tizanidine was implemented, which led to gradual spas-
ticity reduction that allowed rehabilitation program reimplementa-
tion. As a result, the patient’s lower extremity strength and range of
motion improved signiﬁcantly, which allowed her to ambulate with
a walker upon discharge.
Discussion: SPS is a rare neurologic disorder with features of an
autoimmune disease characterized by muscle rigidity that waxes
and wanes with concurrent spasms and a heightened sensitivity to
stimuli such as noise, touch, and emotional distress, which can set
off muscle spasms. Patients with SPS produce glutamic acid decar-
boxylase antibodies that affect GABA-mediated inhibition from the
central nervous system. If glutamic acid decarboxylase function is
inhibited signiﬁcantly, then GABA available for these functions is
decreased, and muscles become continuously stimulated by motor
neurons. Based on the described pathophysiology, baclofen and
benzodiazepines are considered ﬁrst-line pharmacologic treatment
for SPS. We believe that physical activity without adequate spastic-
ity management exacerbated the patient’s symptoms, which makes
rehabilitation efforts challenging. Fortunately, tizanidine provided
adequate symptomatic relief that permitted physical and occupa-
tional therapy focused on range of motion preservation, strengthen-
ing, and voluntary movement control.
Conclusions: The rehabilitation treatment program for individ-
uals with SPS should begin with symptom reduction via education
and pharmacotherapy. This should be followed by a carefully de-
veloped exercise program that improves overall function and qual-
ity of life.
Poster 409
Intractable Back Pain Alleviated by a New
Approach to Peripheral Nerve Stimulation: Cross
Talk. A Case Report.
Maryum Raﬁque, DO (Temple University Hospital, Phil-
adelphia, PA, United States); , Syed A. Husain, DO,
Barkha B. Manne, MD, C. Obi Onyewu, MD.
Disclosures: M. Raﬁque, none.
Objective: New conﬁguration method for placement of periph-
eral stimulator leads to treat pain and improve quality of life.
Design: Case report.
Patients or Programs: An 80-year-old man with chronic pain
syndrome.
Program Description: Peripheral nerve stimulation (PNS) is an
established technique used by physicians to treat chronic peripheral
nerve pain conditions that cause functional debility and lessen
quality of life. Although the exact mechanism by which PNS pro-
duces pain relief is unknown, the gate control mechanism and the
inhibition of the spinothalamic tract are thought to play a role. We
present a case of intractable chronic low back pain that resulted
from lumbar spondylosis and after laminectomy. The patient failed
pharmacotherapy, multiple nerve blocks, and radiofrequency abla-
tion with continued pain reported at 8 of 10 on the visual analog
scale and signiﬁcant functional impairment.
Setting: Outpatient pain management clinic.
Interventions: After a successful PNS trial, the patient underwent
standard placement of 2 PNS units and pulse generators to treat a
large area of the low back. Because there was little pain relief, a
revision of the PNS leads was performed in which the 2 medial leads
of the PNS units were extracted along with 1 pulse generator. The
remaining lateral leads were connected to the pulse generator and
formed a complete circuit that covered a larger area.
Main Outcome Measures: Reduction in pain by using the
visual analog scale and improvement in the quality of life.
Results: The newer lead conﬁguration provided excellent pain
relief and improvement in functional status.
Discussion: This is the ﬁrst known case report that discusses
increasing interlead distance and, therefore, improving coverage of
pain, which led to improvement in functional impairment.
